subject: stats
title: Elements of Probability
objectives: Explain the basic concepts and terminology of probability.
Distinguish classical, relative frequency (empirical) and subjective probability.
Apply the addition and multiplication rules of probability, including conditional probability.
Apply Bayes' Theorem and distinguish permutations from combinations.
study:
Probability measures the likelihood that an event will occur, expressed as a number between 0 and 1 inclusive. P = 0 means the event is impossible; P = 1 means it is certain. An Experiment is a process producing a well-defined outcome; the Sample Space (S) is the set of all possible outcomes; an Event is a subset of the sample space. A Simple Event has exactly one outcome, a Compound Event has two or more, and the Complementary Event (A′) consists of every outcome in S that is not in A, so P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

Key termMutually Exclusive events cannot both occur at once, P(A∩B)=0. Exhaustive events together cover the entire sample space. Independent events mean one's occurrence doesn't affect the other's probability; Dependent events mean it does.

Three approaches measure probability. Classical (a priori) probability assumes equally likely outcomes: P(A) = n(A)/n(S), based on logical reasoning, with no experimentation needed. Relative Frequency (empirical/a posteriori) probability is estimated from observed frequency over many trials: P(A) = fA/n — by the Law of Large Numbers, this converges to the true probability as trials increase. Subjective probability relies on personal judgement or expert opinion where neither other approach applies (e.g. 'a 70% chance this recruitment drive succeeds') — used in risk assessment and business forecasting.

Exam tipThe most common CIPM probability error is applying the simplified addition/multiplication rule (for mutually exclusive/independent events) to events that are not actually mutually exclusive or independent. Always check the relationship between events first.

The Addition Rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); for mutually exclusive events, this simplifies to P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), since P(A and B) = 0. The Multiplication Rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A); for independent events, this simplifies to P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Conditional Probability, the chance of B given A has occurred, is P(B|A) = P(A∩B) / P(A).

The Total Probability Rule says that if B1, B2,...,Bn are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, then for any event A: P(A) = ΣP(A|Bi)×P(Bi). Bayes' Theorem reverses conditional probabilities to update a hypothesis given new evidence: P(Bi|A) = [P(A|Bi)×P(Bi)] / Σ[P(A|Bj)×P(Bj)], where P(Bi) is the prior probability, P(A|Bi) the likelihood, and P(Bi|A) the posterior probability — foundational to Bayesian statistics, spam filtering and medical diagnosis.

Finally, counting techniques: a Permutation is an arrangement where order matters (n!/(n−r)!); a Combination is a selection where order does not matter (n!/[r!(n−r)!]) — selecting committee members uses combinations, since order of selection doesn't change the committee formed. By definition, 0! (zero factorial) equals 1.
recap:
• Sample space = all possible outcomes; Event = subset of it; P(A') = 1 - P(A).
  • Mutually exclusive (can't both occur) vs Exhaustive (cover everything) vs Independent (one doesn't affect other's probability).
  • 3 probability types: Classical (n(A)/n(S), equally likely) · Empirical (observed frequency, Law of Large Numbers) · Subjective (judgement/expert opinion).
  • Addition Rule: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A and B); simplifies for mutually exclusive events.
  • Multiplication Rule: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B|A); simplifies for independent events.
  • Conditional probability: P(B|A) = P(A∩B)/P(A).
  • Bayes' Theorem updates a hypothesis's probability given new evidence (prior → posterior).
  • Permutation = order matters; Combination = order doesn't; 0! = 1.

quiz.why: Empirical probability is based on actual observed outcomes across many trials, not pure logical reasoning.

quiz.q: Probability based on personal judgment, experience or expert opinion, used when objective data is unavailable, is called …… probability.
quiz.why: Subjective probability relies on judgement rather than either equally-likely reasoning or observed frequency.

All outcomes shared by A and another event
quiz.why: The complement covers everything in the sample space that A does not, so P(A) and P(A') always sum to 1.
